title: Pause Long Enough to Notice a Good Moment
subtitle: A small savoring practice without forced positivity
description: When something genuinely pleasant is already happening, give it a little deliberate attention instead of rushing past it. This is a conservative savoring practice, not a rule to feel positive or reinterpret difficult experiences.

lifeOsSource.hack: When a genuinely positive experience occurs, pause briefly and attend to the experience itself instead of immediately switching to the next thing.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose a positive experience that is already real: a good meal, a joke, a quiet walk, finishing useful work, music, a kind message, or another ordinary moment. For a short period, stop adding new input. Notice one or two concrete details and what makes the moment worth noticing. Then continue your day. Do not use the exercise to deny an unpleasant feeling or to manufacture gratitude for something that is not good.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did I actually stay with a positive experience for a moment, and did the practice feel useful, neutral, awkward, or forced?
lifeOsSource.reference: Chen et al. (2026) — Systematic review and meta-analysis of savoring interventions

faq.question: Is savoring just positive thinking?
faq.answer: No. This protocol starts with a positive experience that is already happening and asks you to attend to it. It does not require replacing a difficult thought with a positive one or claiming that a bad situation is secretly good.

faq.question: How long should the pause last?
faq.answer: The review does not establish an optimal micro-dose. Included interventions varied substantially in format and duration. Keep the practice simple enough to use naturally rather than turning a pleasant moment into a timed assignment.

faq.question: Does this treat depression or anxiety?
faq.answer: Brali does not make that claim. The meta-analysis included emotional outcomes across diverse adult samples, but the studies were heterogeneous, mostly used self-report, and did not establish this simple Brali implementation as clinical treatment.

faq.question: What if the exercise feels fake?
faq.answer: Stop or make it smaller. Savoring is not compulsory optimism. If there is no positive experience you want to attend to, there is nothing to perform. The useful target is genuine attention, not a mood score.

intro.html: Some positive experiences disappear from attention almost as soon as they arrive. Savoring interventions try to change that relationship: notice, maintain, or deepen attention to a positive experience instead of immediately moving on. A 2026 systematic review and three-level meta-analysis included 20 randomized trials with 4,805 adult participants and found a moderate average effect across emotional outcomes. The evidence is encouraging, but it is not tidy. Statistical heterogeneity was high, around 30% of included studies were rated high risk of bias, most outcomes were self-reported, and interventions varied in format. Brali therefore offers a deliberately small version of the idea, not a claim that one ritual has been proven optimal.

sections.title: 1. Start with something that is actually good
sections.html: Do not search for a silver lining in an experience you dislike. Wait for something positive that already exists: good coffee, a child's joke, finishing a hard task, a useful conversation, warm light, a song, a meal, a view, or a moment of relief. Savoring works with positive experience; forced reframing is a different intervention.

sections.title: 2. Delay the next input for a moment
sections.html: The practical enemy is often immediate replacement. A message arrives, the song ends, the task is done, and the next feed or obligation starts. Pause before adding something new. You do not need a special breathing pattern or a scripted affirmation.

sections.title: 3. Notice something specific
sections.html: Attend to one or two concrete details: what you can see or hear, what exactly felt satisfying, or why this moment matters to you. Specific attention is easier to execute than the instruction to 'be grateful' or 'feel happier.' If words help, name the detail quietly. If they do not, just notice it.

sections.title: 4. Do not make positivity another performance metric
sections.html: You are not required to intensify the feeling. A neutral result is allowed. Difficult emotions can coexist with a good moment, and savoring does not cancel them. If the practice becomes pressure to feel better, it has drifted away from its useful purpose.

sections.title: 5. Keep the evidence boundary visible
sections.html: The 2026 review found a positive pooled effect, but studies differed substantially and most measured outcomes with questionnaires. Point estimates were smaller against active controls than passive controls, although control type did not reach statistical significance as a moderator. The median intervention duration was about two weeks, not a single five-second pause. This Brali protocol is therefore a conservative implementation of the core savoring idea. Keep it if it makes positive experiences easier to notice without feeling artificial.

references.title: Effectiveness of savoring interventions: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.claim_scope: Supports a positive average effect of savoring interventions on emotional outcomes across 20 randomized trials and 4,805 adults. The evidence is heterogeneous, relies mainly on self-report, includes varied intervention formats, and does not establish this specific micro-practice, an optimal duration, or a clinical treatment effect.

editorialCuration.reason: Translate a fully reviewed 2026 RCT-only savoring meta-analysis into a minimal nonclinical practice. The article explicitly separates the supported savoring construct from Brali's concrete implementation and avoids forced-positivity, dosage, long-term, and treatment claims.
